# Introduction

A classifier can be accurate for the wrong reason: instead of the feature that
defines a class, it may exploit an easier predictive shortcut that works on
the training data and on standard benchmarks but fails when conditions change
[@geirhos2020]. The cue is a spurious correlation, and relying on it is called
shortcut learning (also known as the Clever Hans effect).

This matters because the failure is invisible in the usual evaluation. A
dermoscopy network for melanoma recognition gave higher melanoma scores to
lesions with gentian violet surgical skin markings: its specificity fell from
84.1% for unmarked to 45.8% for marked lesions, and heat maps linked the
markings to the increase [@winkler2019]. Such a model looks accurate on a test
set from the same source, but it cannot be trusted on images that differ in
the cue.

We inject an artificial colour shortcut into MNIST and ask three questions.
(1) How strongly does a network rely on it, depending on the architecture and
the strength of the correlation? (2) Can mitigation at the data level or at
the loss level remove the reliance? (3) Can explainability methods reveal it?

# Literature Review

Geirhos et al. describe shortcut learning as a common problem of deep
learning across several fields [@geirhos2020]. For images, they showed that
ImageNet-trained CNNs depend heavily on texture while humans rely mainly on
shape, and that training on Stylized-ImageNet shifts a network towards shape
and improves robustness [@geirhos2019].

Mitigation can act on the data or on the training objective. Idrissi et al.
show that simply balancing classes and groups, by subsampling or reweighting,
matches state-of-the-art worst-group-accuracy methods while training faster and
needing no additional hyperparameters [@idrissi2022]. Counterfactually
augmented data, introduced for text, are documents that annotators revise so
that the label flips with minimal changes, which can make models less
sensitive to spurious patterns [@kaushik2020]. Just Train Twice needs no group
labels: it upsamples the examples that a first model fits poorly and retrains
[@liu2021]. To inspect what a model uses, we apply Grad-CAM [@selvaraju2016],
Integrated Gradients [@sundararajan2017] and LIME [@ribeiro2016].

# Methods

## Dataset Preparation

We use MNIST (60,000 training and 10,000 test digits) and paint each digit in
one of ten colours, one per class. In the biased training set a digit receives
the colour of its class with probability $p$ and a random colour otherwise. A
random colour is correct one time in ten, so the colour matches the class in
$p + (1-p)/10$ of the images: 55%, 91% and 99.1% for $p = 0.5$, $0.9$ and
$0.99$. A clean training set, the grayscale digit repeated in three channels,
serves as control.

Each model is evaluated on four test sets built from the same 10,000 test
digits, which differ only in colour: *aligned* (the colour of the digit's
class), *clean* (no colour), *random* (a random colour) and *conflicting* (the
colour of class $(y+1) \bmod 10$). We report accuracy on each, the *shortcut
rate* (the share of conflicting images predicted as the colour's digit) and
the *gap* (accuracy on aligned minus accuracy on conflicting images); a large
gap means the model follows the colour.

## Model Training and Evaluation

We compare a fully connected network (MLP, 103,982 parameters) with a small
CNN (106,154 parameters); the MLP has one hidden layer of 44 units so that
both models have almost the same size. The CNN has two blocks of convolution
($3 \times 3$), ReLU and max pooling with 16 and 32 filters, followed by linear
layers $1568 \to 64 \to 10$. All 39 trainings use one shared loop
(cross-entropy, Adam with learning rate $10^{-3}$, batch size 128, 5 epochs)
and seeds 0, 1 and 2; we report mean ± standard deviation over the seeds.

The experiment has two steps. First we train baselines on clean data and on
biased data ($p = 0.5$, $0.9$, $0.99$). Then we apply three mitigations to the
CNN at $p = 0.9$ and $0.99$, keeping model, optimiser, epochs and test sets
unchanged. *Augmentation* paints each digit with a new random colour every
time it is read, always starting from the original grayscale digit, because
recolouring an already coloured digit could keep a brightness that depends on
the old colour and therefore on the class. *Rebalancing* adds conflicting
copies, the same digit painted in a colour that is never its class, until the
colour matches the label in 50% of the images. *Reweighting* keeps the data
and changes the loss: samples whose colour differs from the label get weight
10, all others weight 1, and the loss is the mean of the weighted per-sample
cross-entropy. It needs the shortcut label of every training image.

# Results

**Baselines.** Biased models reach 99--100% on aligned images, higher than the
clean-trained models (95.2% and 96.3%) (@tbl-baseline). Clean-trained models
show no gap (-1.1 and -1.0 points). At $p = 0.9$ the MLP has a gap of 17.4
points and the CNN of 6.4. For the CNN the gap is 1.8 points at $p = 0.5$,
6.4 at $p = 0.9$ and 41.9 at $p = 0.99$, where accuracy on conflicting images
is 58.0% (97.2% for the clean-trained CNN) and the shortcut rate is 28.3%.

| model | training | $p$ | aligned | conflicting | shortcut rate | gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| MLP | clean | -- | 95.2 ± 0.6 | 96.3 ± 0.2 | 0.3 ± 0.1 | -1.1 ± 0.5 |
| MLP | biased | 0.9 | 99.0 ± 0.0 | 81.6 ± 1.3 | 6.4 ± 0.6 | 17.4 ± 1.3 |
| CNN | clean | -- | 96.3 ± 0.4 | 97.2 ± 0.9 | 0.2 ± 0.1 | -1.0 ± 1.3 |
| CNN | biased | 0.5 | 99.1 ± 0.1 | 97.3 ± 0.1 | 0.6 ± 0.1 | 1.8 ± 0.1 |
| CNN | biased | 0.9 | 99.6 ± 0.1 | 93.2 ± 0.3 | 2.7 ± 0.3 | 6.4 ± 0.2 |
| CNN | biased | 0.99 | 99.9 ± 0.0 | 58.0 ± 4.6 | 28.3 ± 5.7 | 41.9 ± 4.6 |

: Test accuracy (%) and shortcut measures without mitigation, mean ± std over
3 seeds. {#tbl-baseline}

## Data mitigation

Augmentation gives 98.3 ± 0.2% on all four test sets at both values of $p$,
with a gap of 0.0, but its accuracy on aligned images is lower than in the
baseline (99.6% at $p = 0.9$, 99.9% at $p = 0.99$). Rebalancing reaches 98.0%
($p = 0.9$) and 98.3% ($p = 0.99$) on conflicting images, with gaps of 1.2 and
1.0 points and 99.3% and 99.2% on aligned images. It enlarges the training set
from 60,000 to about 109,000 and 119,000 images (@tbl-mitigation).

## Model mitigation

Reweighting with weight 10 raises accuracy on conflicting images from 93.2% to
95.5% at $p = 0.9$ (gap from 6.4 to 2.9 points) and from 58.0% to 80.8% at
$p = 0.99$ (gap from 41.9 to 18.6 points). Aligned accuracy is 98.4% and
99.4%. It keeps 60,000 training samples.

| $p$ | method | aligned | clean | conflicting | gap |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.9 | none | 99.6 ± 0.1 | 93.1 ± 1.8 | 93.2 ± 0.3 | 6.4 ± 0.2 |
| 0.9 | augmentation | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 0.0 ± 0.0 |
| 0.9 | rebalancing | 99.3 ± 0.1 | 98.5 ± 0.1 | 98.0 ± 0.2 | 1.2 ± 0.1 |
| 0.9 | reweighting | 98.4 ± 0.2 | 96.6 ± 0.2 | 95.5 ± 0.3 | 2.9 ± 0.4 |
| 0.99 | none | 99.9 ± 0.0 | 67.2 ± 5.7 | 58.0 ± 4.6 | 41.9 ± 4.6 |
| 0.99 | augmentation | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 0.0 ± 0.0 |
| 0.99 | rebalancing | 99.2 ± 0.1 | 98.5 ± 0.1 | 98.3 ± 0.2 | 1.0 ± 0.1 |
| 0.99 | reweighting | 99.4 ± 0.0 | 83.6 ± 5.1 | 80.8 ± 1.3 | 18.6 ± 1.3 |

: All mitigations, test accuracy (%), mean ± std over 3 seeds. The gap is
averaged per seed, so it can differ by 0.1 from the rounded difference.
{#tbl-mitigation}

## Explainable AI

We applied Grad-CAM, which turns the gradients flowing into the last
convolutional layer into a coarse heatmap [@selvaraju2016], and Integrated
Gradients, which accumulates gradients along a path from a baseline input to
score every input feature [@sundararajan2017], to the baseline and the three
mitigated models. LIME fits a simple model around a single prediction
[@ribeiro2016]. The heatmaps are saved in the repository (folder
`results/xai`) and are not reproduced here.

# Discussion

The baselines match the definition of shortcut learning [@geirhos2020]: a
normal test set hides the shortcut, because biased models are best on aligned
images, and the reliance grows with the strength of the correlation. Two
results were unexpected. The MLP follows the colour more than the CNN of the
same size; a possible reason, which we did not test, is that convolutional
filters respond to local shape. And the clean-trained models reach lower
accuracy on aligned images than the biased ones (95.2% and 96.3% against about
99%), so the colour also helps when it is reliable.

Randomising the shortcut, as Stylized-ImageNet does for texture
[@geirhos2019], worked completely here: augmentation removes the gap, but at the
price of aligned accuracy (98.3%), because colour is no longer a useful cue.
Rebalancing is related to data balancing [@idrissi2022] and to counterfactual
augmentation [@kaushik2020], since the added copies change only the colour. It
leaves a gap of about 1 point, perhaps because the training correlation is
still 0.5, which we did not test. Reweighting helps less than we expected from
the results of Idrissi et al. A reason is visible in the weights: at
$p = 0.99$ only 0.9% of the training images are conflicting, so with weight 10
they carry about 8.3% of the total weight (49.7% at $p = 0.9$). Equal total
weight would need a weight of about 110, which we did not try, so this
comparison holds for the fixed weight only.

Further caveats: rebalancing uses about twice as many images and gradient
steps, so part of its gain may come from more data; augmentation needs the
original digits and the knowledge that colour is the shortcut, rarely available
for real shortcuts; and with three seeds and at most 0.5 points between them
we do not rank augmentation and rebalancing. The results come from one
dataset, one known synthetic shortcut and two small architectures. Unknown
shortcuts, as in the skin-marking example, are a harder problem that our
experiments do not address, and this note does not evaluate the heatmaps, so
question (3) stays open here.
